newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: ICO's Lodder sees stable coffee prices for now.
newsitem.headline: ICO's Lodder sees stable coffee prices for now.

text.p: Celsius Lodder, executive director of the International Coffee Organization, said he sees mostly sideways trading on world coffee markets this summer with little real price action to speak of.

Speaking in an extensive interview, Lodder stressed that volatility was an unavoidable part of any commodities market, however, and he said the ICO would be willing to provide country-by-country crop forecasts to help curb wild price swings if its 64 members asked it to do so.

"If you look at the market now you see a certain balance, everything is pointing to a certain equilibrium for the next months," Lodder said. "There's no reason why prices should go up or down," he added, saying he expected to see little or no price action until September when Colombia's harvest gets under way and Brazil's ends.

The only current elements of concern, according to Lodder, is that consumer stocks are too low to confront any serious disruption in the flow of coffee from producers and the fact that Brazil's current crop size remains shrouded in mystery.
Lodder visited this industrial hub in northwest Colombia for an event Tuesday marking the 70th anniversary of Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation.

Unlike many analysts, he stopped short of criticizing the "just-in-time" import policy recently adopted by major roasters, telling Reuters he viewed it as a necessity in an increasingly competitive market where a big premium has been placed on cutting costs.
"It's a need, they need to do it, they need to reduce costs," he said.

He conceded the "just-in-time" policy was one of the driving forces behind "the price explosion earlier this year," saying the surge stemmed from the fact that roasters were working with too short a turnover period and panicked when Colombia was hit by a crippling strike. But with the right "pre-conditions" the policy can work, he said.
As for forecasts, Lodder said he was aware of and welcomed plans by Brazil to revamp its crop forecasting system by next year.

"This is one of the things that we need to fine tune or to improve," he said. "We need to have this, otherwise we have only one forecast, and that's the USDA's," he added, saying it was sure to help "calm down the market."
Lodder said the ICO was ideally positioned to provide crop forecasts as well, however, and would be more than willing to do so if its members ask it to.

"We are in a unique position to provide information to the market," he said, adding that the ICO could undoubtedly provide much more reliable numbers than the USDA. "So far they (ICO members) don't want us to do any forecasts. But it's a point that I think in the future they'll start to see -- we must use this wealth of information that we have."
He did not elaborate on how soon the ICO might actually get into the forecasting business. But he stressed that information held the key to taking some of the volatility out of the coffee market.

"The first condition for a free market is transparency ... But you only reach transparency if you have information in the market, if you have the statistics on how much you produce, how much you export, how much you have in stocks."
Even in the best of all possible worlds, Lodder said volatility was unlikely to disappear, however.
"Volatility is part of the market, you have to learn how to live with this problem. You have to learn how to hedge yourself," he said.
While speculative funds are part of the problem they give the market sorely needed liquidity, he said, adding that there was no point in trying to rein them in or place new curbs on trading activity.

"They're part of the market, they're part of the price determination," Lodder said. "I don't think that if you impose any plans or controls that it will help, it will not avoid volatility. Don't blame the thermometer for the fever."
